beats.narration: There was a time when you could take off from London in the morning and land in New York earlier, by the local clock, than when you left.
The crossing took about three and a half hours, roughly half the time of an ordinary jet. The aircraft that made it possible was Concorde.

props.label: London to New York: about 3 h 30 min

beats.narration: For twenty-seven years it was the fastest way for a passenger to cross an ocean. Then, in two thousand and three, it simply stopped. So what went wrong?

props.title: Why Concorde Stopped Flying
props.subtitle: 27 years at twice the speed of sound, and then it was gone

beats.narration: Concorde began with a treaty signed in nineteen sixty-two. Britain and France agreed to build a supersonic airliner together, with assembly lines in Filton, near Bristol, and in Toulouse.
The prototype first flew in nineteen sixty-nine. In service, Concorde cruised at Mach two point oh four, about two thousand one hundred and eighty kilometres an hour.

props.label: Cruising speed: more than twice the speed of sound

beats.narration: It flew as high as sixty thousand feet. From up there, passengers could see the curve of the Earth, under a sky turning dark blue.

props.label: Maximum cruising altitude
props.note: about 18 km, high enough to see the curve of the Earth

beats.narration: Air friction heated the skin so much that the nose reached about one hundred and twenty-seven degrees Celsius, and the whole airframe stretched by several inches in flight.
Airlines were excited. In the nineteen sixties, sixteen carriers took out options on more than seventy aircraft. Supersonic travel looked like the future.

props.text: Sixteen airlines took out options on more than seventy Concordes.

beats.narration: Then almost all of them walked away. In early nineteen seventy-three, Pan Am cancelled its options and others followed. The oil crisis made fuel expensive, and the noise made Concorde unwelcome.
In the end, only twenty Concordes were built, and just fourteen of them carried passengers: seven with British Airways and seven with Air France.

props.label: Concordes built
props.note: Only 14 flew for airlines: 7 with British Airways, 7 with Air France

beats.narration: And there was a bigger problem: the sonic boom. In nineteen seventy-three, the United States banned civil supersonic flight over land, so Concorde could only fly fast over the sea.
Passenger service began on the twenty-first of January, nineteen seventy-six. British Airways flew to Bahrain, while Air France flew to Rio de Janeiro.
But the numbers never really worked. Concorde carried about one hundred passengers. A Boeing jumbo jet carried around four hundred, and used far less fuel for every seat.
So tickets were expensive. In two thousand and three, a standard return ticket between London and New York cost about six thousand six hundred pounds.

props.label: Standard London to New York return fare, 2003

beats.narration: Its regulars were bankers, celebrities and executives, people for whom time was worth more than money. For British Airways, Concorde even made an operating profit for years.

props.text: Bankers, celebrities and executives: people for whom time was worth more than money.

beats.narration: Then, on the twenty-fifth of July, two thousand, Air France Flight forty-five ninety began its take-off from Paris Charles de Gaulle, bound for New York.

On the runway lay a strip of metal that had fallen from another airliner minutes earlier. Concorde's tyre hit it and burst. Debris struck the wing, a fuel tank ruptured, and the leaking fuel caught fire.

props.text: A metal strip dropped by another jet burst a tyre. Debris struck the wing, a fuel tank ruptured, and the fuel caught fire.

beats.narration: Less than two minutes after take-off, the aircraft crashed into a hotel in Gonesse. All one hundred and nine people on board and four people on the ground were killed.

props.label: Lives lost
props.note: 109 on board and 4 on the ground

beats.narration: It was the only fatal accident in Concorde's history, but it destroyed the aircraft's reputation for perfect safety. The whole fleet was grounded for more than a year.
Engineers lined the fuel tanks with Kevlar and rubber, fitted tougher Michelin tyres and protected the wiring in the landing gear bay. Concorde was cleared to fly again.

props.title: The fixes
items: Protected wiring in the gear bay

beats.narration: It returned to service on the seventh of November, two thousand and one, just eight weeks after the September eleventh attacks had plunged air travel into a deep slump.
Premium travellers were slow to come back, and the aircraft were getting old. Airbus, which supported the fleet, said keeping them flying would need costly extra maintenance.
In April two thousand and three, Air France and British Airways announced that Concorde would retire. The last commercial flight landed at Heathrow on the twenty-fourth of October.
Concorde did not disappear because it was too fast. It disappeared because speed alone could not pay for a tiny, ageing fleet that burned so much fuel for every passenger.

Since then, no airliner has carried passengers faster than sound. But in twenty twenty-six, American regulators proposed lifting their old ban on supersonic flight over land. The question Concorde left behind is open again.

props.title: Supersonic, Again?
props.subtitle: In 2026 the FAA proposed lifting its ban on supersonic flight over land
